newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Thyssen poised to reap restructuring gains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thyssen poised to reap restructuring gains.

text.p: German steel group Thyssen AG on Tuesday predicted a hike in its full-year profits after divestment proceeds boosted first-half 1996/97 pre-tax earnings by 81 percent to 631 million marks ($372.6 million).
The divestments also caused sales in the six months to March 31 to fall 2.7 percent to 17.9 billion marks and lowered orders 1.6 percent to 17.8 billion marks, Thyssen said.
But the company said its improved business structure would lead to "a distinct business upswing" in the second half of the year ending September 30.
"The restructuring measures are beginning to bear fruit," the company said in a statement.
Adjusted for the effects of the divestments, sales rose two percent and pre-tax profit 22 percent, Thyssen said.
At 1000 GMT Thyssen shares were up six marks at 398.50 marks, with the blue-chip DAX index up 0.3 percent at 3,668.92.
Even without the effect of its divestments, Thyssen had a solid first half and was on track to see profit rise next year, said Merrill Lynch analyst Alan Coats.

"This is a good result, but it was an intermediate year," he told Reuters. "The big gain should be in 1998. We should see greatly improved steel results based on steel prices going up very sharply, and improvement in capital goods margins."
Weak steel prices eroded profit from Thyssen's stainless steel operation in the first half of 1996/97, Coats said.

Thyssen has sold off defence, pumps, coal and metals businesses to focus on its elevator, auto parts, flat steel, production systems and raw materials units. It has also agreed to merge its steel operations with rival Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp.

It forecast an improved result this year in its trading and services and capital goods divisions. Steel operations would also post a clearly positive result, although it was not yet clear whether it would match the level of a year ago.
Thyssen hoped to pay an at least unchanged dividend after cutting its payout to eight marks last year.
In the first half, sales in capital goods and manufacturing activities rose three percent to 5.59 billion marks, while revenue in trading and services slipped 1.6 percent to 8.85 billion marks.

Steel revenue was down 13 percent to 4.65 billion marks due to price pressure and Thyssen's departure from long steel production. But it said demand was strong and raw steel production climbed nine percent in the first half.
The number of employees was down eight percent to 112,893 workers.
